title: Optimizing discriminator to completion is prohibitive
description: Optimizing D to completion in the inner loop of training is computationally prohibitive and would result in overfitting on finite datasets, so an iterative alternation must be used instead.
canonical_description: full inner-loop discriminator optimization computationally prohibitive and overfits

evidence.quote:
Optimizing $D$ to completion in the
inner loop of training is computationally prohibitive,

verdict.reasoning: All three deep-read papers are assessed as not_addressed, and the assessments are consistent and specific. Paper 1 analyzes GAN generalization and equilibrium while taking the alternating training protocol as given; its best-response cycling examples concern non-convergence of full optimization, not the computational cost or finite-sample overfitting of completing the inner-loop discriminator update. Paper 2 is diagnostic work on discriminator under/overfitting in WGANs, but its independent discriminator is trained offline for measurement after the generator is fixed, not as a replacement for or mitigation of full inner-loop optimization. Paper 3 reframes GANs as a Lagrangian saddle-point problem and proves convergence of alternating primal-dual updates, but again assumes the standard single-step alternation and abstracts away finite-capacity/finite-data regimes. None of the papers analyzes why full inner-loop discriminator optimization is computationally prohibitive, characterizes an appropriate number of discriminator steps, proposes a feasible scheme for optimizing D to completion, or justifies the alternation schedule. The gap's specific problem therefore remains untouched.

paper.title: Generalization and Equilibrium in Generative Adversarial Nets (GANs)
paper.abstract: We show that training of generative adversarial network (GAN) may not have good generalization properties; e.g., training may appear successful but the trained distribution may be far from target distribution in standard metrics. However, generalization does occur for a weaker metric called neural net distance. It is also shown that an approximate pure equilibrium exists in the discriminator/generator game for a special class of generators with natural training objectives when generator capacity and training set sizes are moderate. This existence of equilibrium inspires MIX+GAN protocol, which can be combined with any existing GAN training, and empirically shown to improve some of them.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper is a GAN theory paper on two distinct questions: (1) whether GAN training generalizes, showing that JS/Wasserstein distances can fail to generalize on finite samples while a weaker "neural net distance" does generalize, and (2) whether approximate pure equilibria exist in the generator/discriminator game, proved for mixtures of generators and for enlarged (k+1-layer, ~p^2 parameter) generator nets, plus the heuristic MIX+GAN. It also gives toy examples where best-response dynamics (optimizing each player to optimality) cycle and fail to converge. None of these contributions addresses how or whether to optimize the discriminator to completion in the inner loop, or why an iterative alternation must be used instead.
assessments.what_remains_open: The specific gap — that full inner-loop discriminator optimization is computationally prohibitive and would overfit on finite datasets, so iterative alternation must be used — is not tackled. The paper takes the standard alternating training procedure as given and analyzes its generalization and equilibrium properties; it does not analyze the computational cost of running D to completion, does not characterize how many (k) discriminator steps suffice, does not propose or justify an alternation schedule, and does not connect the finite-sample overfitting failure modes it identifies (JS/Wasserstein memorization, low-capacity discriminators missing diversity) to the burden of completing the inner-loop D optimization. Its best-response examples concern non-convergence/cycling of full optimization rather than computational prohibitive-ness or finite-sample overfitting of the inner-loop D update.

paper.title: Investigating Under and Overfitting in Wasserstein Generative Adversarial Networks
paper.abstract: We investigate under and overfitting in Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), using discriminators unseen by the generator to measure generalization. We find that the model capacity of the discriminator has a significant effect on the generator's model quality, and that the generator's poor performance coincides with the discriminator underfitting. Contrary to our expectations, we find that generators with large model capacities relative to the discriminator do not show evidence of overfitting on CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and CelebA.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper is an empirical study of under/overfitting in Wasserstein GANs. It introduces auxiliary and independent discriminators (trained on data unseen by the generator, or on an independent held-out split) to measure discriminator generalization and generator model quality, and it varies discriminator capacity. Its main findings are that the alternation-trained original discriminator underfits/fails to generalize on test data while auxiliary/independent discriminators show little generalization gap, and that generator overfitting is not observed on CIFAR10/100/CelebA. This is adjacent diagnostic work about discriminator generalization, but it does not address the problem of making full inner-loop discriminator optimization tractable during GAN training.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap's specific problem — that optimizing the discriminator to completion in the inner loop of GAN training is computationally prohibitive and would overfit finite datasets, so iterative alternation is required — is not addressed. The paper never proposes or evaluates a procedure for full inner-loop discriminator optimization while training the generator; its "independent discriminator" is trained offline (100K SGD steps) after a generator is fixed, purely to estimate a divergence for measurement, not to replace the inner-loop optimization. It likewise does nothing to mitigate the computational cost of full discriminator training or to justify reducing the number of alternation steps. Thus the question of how to make full inner-loop discriminator optimization feasible, or how to avoid the overfitting/prohibitive-cost tradeoff that motivates alternation, remains entirely open.

paper.title: Training Generative Adversarial Networks via Primal-Dual Subgradient Methods: A Lagrangian Perspective on GAN
paper.abstract: We relate the minimax game of generative adversarial networks (GANs) to finding the saddle points of the Lagrangian function for a convex optimization problem, where the discriminator outputs and the distribution of generator outputs play the roles of primal variables and dual variables, respectively. This formulation shows the connection between the standard GAN training process and the primal-dual subgradient methods for convex optimization. The inherent connection does not only provide a theoretical convergence proof for training GANs in the function space, but also inspires a novel objective function for training. The modified objective function forces the distribution of generator outputs to be updated along the direction according to the primal-dual subgradient methods. A toy example shows that the proposed method is able to resolve mode collapse, which in this case cannot be avoided by the standard GAN or Wasserstein GAN. Experiments on both Gaussian mixture synthetic data and real-world image datasets demonstrate the performance of the proposed method on generating diverse samples.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper reinterprets the GAN minimax game as finding saddle points of the Lagrangian of a convex program (discriminator outputs as primal variables, generator-output distribution as dual variables), proves convergence of alternating primal-dual subgradient updates in function space when discriminator/generator have enough capacity, and proposes a modified generator loss that pushes the generated probability distribution along the optimal dual direction to mitigate mode collapse. Its main contributions are theoretical convergence guarantees (in an idealized convex, full-capacity setting) and a mode-collapse-avoiding training objective, validated on toy/Gaussian-mixture data, MNIST, and CIFAR-10.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap concerns the reason full inner-loop discriminator optimization is infeasible — computational cost and overfitting on finite datasets — and the consequent need for iterative alternation. The paper does not analyze or address this problem: it takes the standard alternating protocol as given (k0 = 1 single-step discriminator updates in all experiments), never studies the cost or the overfitting induced by training D to completion, and does not propose any scheme or analysis related to discriminator overfitting on finite data. Its convergence theorem instead assumes an idealized function-space convex optimization with full-capacity networks and an adequate step-size schedule, assumptions that abstract away precisely the finite-capacity/finite-data regime where the gap's problem arises. Mode collapse (a different failure mode) is the actual target of the proposed generator-objective change, so the specific problem in this gap remains untouched.

ranking.feasibility_reasoning: Making concrete progress is feasible without fundamental breakthroughs or frontier-scale compute. The needed data are standard/synthetic GAN benchmarks (MNIST, CIFAR, toy distributions), so no costly collection or labeling is required, and small-to-mid-scale GAN training runs on a single modest GPU. Methodologically, the gap can be addressed by extending existing GAN-training analyses: sweep and characterize inner-loop discriminator steps, measure discriminator convergence versus finite-sample overfitting, and derive/evaluate early-stopping or scheduling rules. The scope can be narrowed to specific model families and datasets, and success is measurable via discriminator generalization gaps, training time to convergence, and downstream generator metrics such as FID. The main feasibility limits are that "computationally prohibitive" is context-dependent and a fully general theoretical characterization may remain hard, so the strongest tractable contribution is likely a well-controlled empirical/theoretical study rather than a universal proof.
